{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"A device isn’t fully owned if the company that sold it can reach through the sale and switch off what you bought. That sounds like a technical dispute about licenses, firmware, or server access. It isn’t. It’s a dispute about whether ownership means control, or merely permission that can be revoked by somebody else.

You can hold the phone, tractor, car, camera, or medical device in your hands. You can pay the invoice, insure it, repair it, and pass it to somebody you trust. Yet if a remote command can remove a feature after the transaction, your control is conditional. The device has a second owner, invisible and very much alive, sitting in a corporate control room.

Of course, makers have legitimate reasons to patch security flaws, correct dangerous defects, and stop an abusive use of their networks. We shouldn’t confuse a safety update with a company’s power to withdraw a promised capability. The question is narrower: when a feature was part of the product you chose and paid for, what gives the seller the right to make it disappear?

The usual answer is that you didn’t buy the feature. You bought access to software, and access remains subject to the terms you accepted. But that answer turns an ordinary purchase into a subscription without using the word subscription. It makes the customer responsible for the price and the risk while reserving the decisive power for the maker.

Imagine buying a set of tools whose handles are fitted with locks. The tools work when the manufacturer approves your account; they stop working when the manufacturer changes its business plan. You still own the metal, the case, and the receipt. You just can’t use the thing for the purpose that made it valuable. That isn’t ownership in any meaningful consumer sense. It’s a hostage situation with better branding.

I think this matters even when the maker says most customers will never notice. Ownership isn’t measured by how often a power is exercised. A landlord who rarely enters your apartment without permission still has a different relationship to the space than a company that can enter whenever it likes. We understand this instinctively in physical property, but we’ve allowed software to smuggle the exception into every room.

And what happens when the company is sold, goes bankrupt, abandons a product, or decides that a new business model is more profitable? You may have done everything right and still lose the feature because the institution controlling it changed hands. The device doesn’t become less real. Your ownership becomes less real.

Sure, a maker can say that remote control protects the ecosystem. But an ecosystem that depends on permanent obedience isn’t a community; it’s a dependency. If your car’s heated seats, your camera’s processing mode, or your equipment’s basic function can be disabled from afar, you’re not buying a finished object. You’re renting a temporary arrangement of permissions, and the damn receipt is camouflage.

We should write the rule plainly: a sale transfers meaningful control. A maker may fix security problems, but it shouldn’t be able to revoke ordinary functionality merely because it can. You should be able to keep using the product you bought, maintain it, and transfer it without asking a distant server for permission. I can accept limits that protect other people from concrete harm; I can’t accept a definition of ownership that excludes the owner.

The point isn’t nostalgia for gadgets that never change. It’s a demand that change remain accountable to the person who paid for the thing. When you buy a device, you’re buying a piece of the world that should answer to you. If it can be switched off after sale, then the sale transferred possession, not ownership. We ought to stop calling that ownership until the maker has surrendered the switch.","omitted":[],"refused":""}
